newsitem.title: BULGARIA: IMF team due in Sofia for currency board talks.
newsitem.headline: IMF team due in Sofia for currency board talks.

text.p: International Monetary Fund (IMF) negotiators are due in Bulgaria on Monday to discuss preparations for a strict fixed exchange rate regime which aims to stabilise the collapsing economy.
IMF mission leader Anne McGuirk is scheduled to arrive in the evening from Brussels where the European Union discussed mobilising help for the country.

"An IMF technical mission has been in Sofia since last week to do the preliminary work but negotiations will start with the mission arriving on Monday," an IMF official who declined to be named told Reuters.

The team is expected to review Bulgaria's slumping economy and set arrangements for a currency board system, proposed last year to halt the freefall of the lev and to restore confidence in banks, one third of which are in receivership.

The system requires levs in circulation to be matched by central bank reserves, severely curbing financial powers of the government and the central bank, and preventing printing of money. It will entail closure of inefficient state enterprises and more job losses.

On Sunday the World Bank said it had $200 million available for Bulgaria if the government speeded up privatisation and closures of loss-making state firms, and lifted price controls on basic goods and services.
Delayed reform and mismanagement by the previous Socialist administration have thrown Bulgaria's economy into chaos, while 30 days of widespread strikes and political squabbling further paralysed it.
Opposition demands for early elections and the refusal of the ruling ex-communists to yield produced a political deadlock which was resolved three weeks ago.
President Petar Stoyanov mediated an agreement to hold general elections on April 19, dissolved parliament and named an interim cabinet headed by Sofia mayor Stefan Sofianski.

Sofianski said Bulgaria needed a currency board and his cabinet will prepare for its implementation. The system's introduction, however, would require amendments to banking laws to be passed by the new parliament, which must also decide whether to peg the lev to the dollar or the mark.
Central bank governor Lyubomir Filipov saw June as the earliest date for its introduction.
One of the last items voted by the outgoing parliament was to expand powers of the interim cabinet to negotiate vital loans and agreements with multilateral lending institutions.

Passing a realistic austerity budget for this year will be one of the first tasks of the new parliament, once elected. Bulgaria's deepening crisis has made obsolete the 1997 budget assumptions drafted by the former Socialist government.
The collapse of the lev has hit all areas of the economy heavily, eroding average wages to the equivalent of around $10 a month.

The currency has fallen by some 300 percent against the dollar since the beginning of the year. Increased foreign currency supply last week helped the lev recover from its February 7 all-time low of 3,200 to the dollar, to trade on Monday at 2,300-2,350 on the interbank foreign exchange market.
Restoring confidence in the lev will need a huge effort, economists say, as companies and individuals prefer to settle payments directly in dollars, despite a ban on domestic hard currency payments.
Month-on-month inflation for January 1 to 25 was 43.8 percent and the Bulgarian Academy of Sciences forecast it would reach nearly 100 percent in February.

The Fund and government will also need to seek means to resolve Bulgaria's 1.7 trillion lev ($770 million) domestic debt, seen as a hindrance to successful implementation of the currency board. ($ = 2210 Bulgarian Levs)
